verses.title: Do not fret
verses.heading: Counsel for those troubled by evildoers' success
verses.meaning: The heading names David, and the psalm opens with two commands: do not fret over those who do evil, and do not envy those who do wrong. The Hebrew verb translated 'fret' can describe becoming heated or agitated. The poem does not deny that wrongdoing may look successful for a time; it warns against letting that sight kindle resentment or a wish to share the wrongdoer's gains. The counsel redirects attention from comparison toward trust and faithful action.
verses.context: Psalm 37 is a wisdom poem and a Hebrew acrostic, offering proverb-like counsel rather than a narrative. Proverbs 24:19–20 gives nearly the same advice, and Psalm 73 tells the story of someone who nearly stumbled through envy of the wicked.
explore: Do not fret
Fretting is a burning inner agitation. The psalm addresses anxiety and resentment directly.
Do not envy
Envy wants what the wrongdoer has. The psalm warns that this desire misleads the heart.
verses.reflect: When others seem to get ahead by doing wrong, how do you react inside? What would it mean not to fret?
verses.alt: A villager quietly tends a small garden while a rich neighbor's mansion rises behind.

verses.title: Like grass
verses.heading: The fleeting success of the wicked
verses.meaning: The reason for the opening command is pictured rather than argued: evildoers will wither like grass and wilt like tender plants. Their apparent success is fragile and temporary. The comparison does not say every wealthy person is wicked or invite pleasure at anyone's fall. It asks the troubled reader to view present appearances from the longer horizon of God's justice and therefore refuse envy.
verses.context: Isaiah 40:6–8 says all flesh is grass that withers, and James 1:10–11 compares the rich to a flower that fades in the sun. In the acrostic, verse 2 belongs to the poem's repeated contrast between passing wrongdoing and God's lasting care.
explore: Wither quickly
The image is of grass scorched by the sun. Success built on wrongdoing does not last.
Tender plants
Fresh green shoots wilt easily. The image stresses fragility.
verses.reflect: What success around you looks impressive now but may not last? How does the long view change your feelings?
verses.alt: Green grass on a hillside wilts under a scorching sun.

verses.title: Trust and do good
verses.heading: An alternative to fretting
verses.meaning: Instead of fretting, the psalm joins trust in the LORD with doing good. Dwelling in the land places the counsel within Israel's covenant inheritance, while 'cultivate faithfulness' pictures steady care rather than anxious comparison. The line does not commend passive waiting: trust becomes visible in good action and dependable living where God has placed His people.
verses.context: Jeremiah 29:4–7 addresses Judean exiles in Babylon, telling them to settle, plant and seek that city's welfare; it is a later situation that illustrates faithful living in an unsettled place. Galatians 6:7–10 urges Christian communities not to grow weary in doing good. Proverbs 3:3–6 connects trust with faithfulness and a path directed by the LORD.
explore: Trust and do good
Trust in God leads to active goodness. Faith is not passive.
Cultivate faithfulness
Faithfulness is grown over time. It requires patient daily care.
verses.reflect: What would cultivating faithfulness look like in your ordinary routine this week?
verses.alt: A farmer patiently tills a small terraced field at dawn.

verses.title: Delight yourself in the LORD
verses.heading: Joy in God shapes desire
verses.meaning: The verse sets delight in the LORD beside the promise that He will give the heart's desires. In this psalm, that delight belongs to a life of trust, goodness and patient hope, not to a technique for obtaining every private wish. The object of delight is the LORD Himself. The promise invites the reader to bring desire into that relationship and receive from God rather than envy what wrongdoers appear to possess.
verses.context: Psalm 16:9–11 locates fullness of joy in God's presence. Isaiah 58:13–14 connects delight in the LORD with honoring Him rather than pursuing one's own pleasure. Matthew 6:31–34 addresses anxious pursuit of necessities and calls Jesus' hearers to seek God's kingdom first; it is a later teaching, not the original setting of Psalm 37.
explore: Delight yourself
Delight is deep joy and pleasure. It is directed toward God Himself.
Desires of your heart
Delighting in God shapes desire. The promise is not a blank check.
verses.reflect: What do you most delight in? How might delighting in God change what you want?
verses.alt: An anonymous person sits contentedly in a flowering orchard, face lifted in joy.

verses.title: Commit your way
verses.heading: Entrusting one's path to God
verses.meaning: To commit one's way to the LORD is literally to roll that path onto Him: to entrust one's course and cause rather than carry them through anxious control. The repeated command to trust keeps commitment from becoming a bargain. 'He will do it' points forward to verse 6, where God brings the person's righteousness and justice into the light. The promise concerns His action and vindication, not a guarantee that every chosen plan will succeed unchanged.
verses.context: Proverbs 16:3 says, 'Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established,' and 1 Peter 5:7 says to cast all your anxiety on Him.
explore: Commit your way
The word suggests rolling a burden onto God. Your path becomes His concern.
He will do it
God acts on behalf of those who trust Him. The outcome is His.
verses.reflect: What plan or path do you need to roll onto God today?
verses.alt: A traveler rolls a heavy stone onto a sturdy cart at the start of a road.

verses.title: Like the dawn
verses.heading: Righteousness revealed in time
verses.meaning: This verse completes the promise of verse 5: the LORD will bring the entrusted person's righteousness and justice into view like dawn becoming noonday. The imagery is one of vindication—what has been obscured is made visible under God's judgment. It does not promise that every human opinion will change on the reader's schedule, nor does it declare anyone sinless. It encourages a righteous cause to be entrusted to God instead of advanced by envy or wrath.
verses.context: Proverbs 4:14–19 contrasts the dark path of the wicked with the righteous path shining brighter toward midday. Isaiah 58:6–10 places dawn-like light beside justice, generosity and care for the oppressed. Malachi 4:1–3 uses sunrise imagery for the future day of the LORD; it is a distinct prophetic setting rather than a prediction of an easy present life.
explore: Like the dawn
Dawn grows steadily brighter. God's vindication may come gradually.
Noonday sun
Noon is the brightest time of day. Justice will be fully visible.
verses.reflect: Is there something about you that you wish others could see clearly? How could you trust God's timing?
verses.alt: Sunlight rises from dawn to full noon over a valley.

verses.title: Be still and wait
verses.heading: Patient trust when wrongdoers prosper
verses.meaning: The reader is told to be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him even when another person's wicked scheme appears to prosper. This stillness restrains agitated reaction; it is patient dependence rather than approval of evil or indifference to those harmed. By repeating 'do not fret,' the verse keeps the focus on refusing resentment and rash imitation while God's justice is awaited.
verses.context: Lamentations 3:24–28 speaks of quietly waiting for the LORD's salvation amid affliction. Isaiah 30:15 contrasts quiet confidence with Judah's refusal and flight to military strength. Psalm 46:8–11 commands stillness in a scene where God ends wars and is exalted among the nations; its wording is a helpful comparison, but its setting is not identical to Psalm 37.
explore: Be still
Stillness is quiet trust. It means ceasing anxious striving.
Wait patiently
Patience trusts God's timing. It does not demand immediate results.
verses.reflect: What would being still before God look like in your current situation?
verses.alt: An anonymous person sits quietly by a calm lake at dawn.

verses.title: Refrain from anger
verses.heading: Fretting leads to harm
verses.meaning: The third warning against fretting is now joined to a command to release anger and abandon wrath. The final clause explains the danger: this agitated course leads only toward harm. The verse is not a prohibition against naming injustice, seeking protection or caring for those who suffer. It warns the reader not to let resentment at evildoers become a new path of wrongdoing.
verses.context: Ephesians 4:25–28 permits anger without sin while warning against giving evil a foothold. James 1:19–21 says human anger does not produce God's righteousness and calls for a receptive, humble response. Proverbs 14:29–30 contrasts patience and tranquility with quick temper and envy.
explore: Abandon wrath
Letting go of anger is a choice. It frees the heart.
It can only bring harm
Fretting and anger lead to wrongdoing. They harm the one who holds them.
verses.reflect: Is there anger you need to release to God? What would letting go look like?
verses.alt: A clenched hand slowly opens to release a stone into a stream.
